name: Dextromethorphan + Phenylephrine + Chlorpheniramine
meta: Per 5 mL: Dextromethorphan HBr 15 mg + Phenylephrine HCl 5 mg +

Dextromethorphan Hydrobromide: Centrally acting non-opioid antitussive; Phenylephrine Hydrochloride: Alpha-1 adrenergic agonist (nasal decongestant); Chlorpheniramine Maleate: First-generation H1 antihistamine (alkylamine)
Dextromethorphan Hydrobromide: R05DA09; Phenylephrine Hydrochloride: R01BA03 (oral decongestant); Chlorpheniramine Maleate: R06AB04
sections: White crystalline powder (hydrobromide), sparingly soluble in water.
White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), freely soluble in water.
White crystalline powder (maleate), freely soluble in water.

Dextromethorphan Hydrobromide: The dextrorotatory isomer of levomethorphan, lacking opioid analgesic activity at normal doses. First approval/introduction: Patented 1949; medical use 1953; US OTC 1958 (Hoffmann-La Roche). Phenylephrine Hydrochloride: In September 2023 a US FDA advisory committee concluded oral phenylephrine is ineffective as a nasal decongestant at OTC doses; in November 2024 the FDA proposed removing it from the OTC monograph. First approval/introduction: Patented 1933; medical use from 1938. Chlorpheniramine Maleate: One of the most widely used first-generation antihistamines; on the WHO List of Essential Medicines. First approval/introduction: Patented 1948; medical use from 1949 (Schering).
Per 5 mL: Dextromethorphan HBr 15 mg + Phenylephrine HCl 5 mg +
Dextromethorphan suppresses cough centrally; phenylephrine decongests the nasal mucosa; chlorpheniramine reduces rhinorrhoea and sneezing.

Dextromethorphan Hydrobromide Acts on the medullary cough centre (sigma-1 agonist, NMDA antagonist) to raise the cough threshold; lacks analgesic and respiratory-depressant effects at therapeutic doses. Receptor / target profile: Sigma-1 agonist, NMDA receptor antagonist and serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor acting on the medullary cough centre.

Phenylephrine Hydrochloride Stimulates alpha-1 receptors in nasal mucosal blood vessels, causing vasoconstriction and reducing nasal congestion. Receptor / target profile: Selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist causing vasoconstriction; minimal beta activity.

Chlorpheniramine Maleate Competitive H1 antagonist with anticholinergic action, reducing rhinorrhoea, sneezing, itching and lacrimation. Receptor / target profile: Potent H1 inverse agonist with weak antimuscarinic activity and some serotonin reuptake inhibition.
Summary: Rapidly absorbed; Tmax 2–2.5 h. Metabolised by CYP2D6 to dextrorphan. Half-life 3–4 h (longer in poor metabolisers).
Gut wall and hepatic – MAO-A/B, sulfation, glucuronidation
Summary: Oral bioavailability ~38% (gut-wall metabolism by MAO). Half-life 2–3 h.
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax 2.5–6 h. Hepatic metabolism. Half-life 12–43 h.
Symptomatic relief of dry, non-productive cough with nasal congestion, runny nose and sneezing due to common cold, allergic rhinitis or upper respiratory infection
Adults and children >12 years: 5–10 mL three to four times daily
Children 6–12 years: 2.5–5 mL three times daily
Not recommended for children under 4 years
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Not for <2 years; 2–6 years per specialist.
Use with or within 14 days of MAO inhibitors
Severe hypertension, severe coronary artery disease
Use with or within 14 days of MAO inhibitors
Concomitant or recent (14 days) MAO inhibitors
Chronic cough with excessive sputum – do not suppress
SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine – CYP2D6 inhibition and serotonin syndrome)
Chlorpheniramine Maleate: With food; avoid alcohol.

Dextromethorphan Hydrobromide: Excitation, confusion, hallucinations, ataxia, respiratory depression. Naloxone may help; supportive care. Phenylephrine Hydrochloride: Hypertension, reflex bradycardia, headache, seizures. Alpha-blocker (phentolamine) for severe hypertension. Chlorpheniramine Maleate: CNS depression or excitation (children), anticholinergic effects, convulsions. Supportive care.
Cochrane (Smith et al., 2014) – insufficient evidence for or against OTC cough medicines.
US FDA advisory committee (2023) – oral phenylephrine ineffective as a decongestant.
Avoid if you have uncontrolled high BP
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
